faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Everything you need to know about using Dealeg
faq.q1: Are the coupon codes on Dealeg free to use?
faq.a1: Yes, completely free. Dealeg is free for everyone. You simply find a coupon code, copy it, and use it at checkout on the merchant's site. We earn a small commission from merchants when you make a purchase through our links, at no extra cost to you.
faq.q2: How do I use a coupon code?
faq.a2: Click the "Get Code" button on any coupon. This copies the code to your clipboard and opens the merchant's website. Paste the code in the promo or coupon field at checkout to apply your discount.
faq.a3: We make every effort to list only working codes, and our community votes on whether codes are still valid. However, merchants control their offers, so codes can expire or change. Each code shows verification status and votes to help you find working ones.
faq.q4: How often are new deals added?
faq.a4: We update deals regularly. New coupons and offers are added as they become available, and expired ones are removed. Subscribe to our newsletter to get the latest deals delivered to your inbox.
faq.q5: Is Dealeg available in my language?
faq.a5: Dealeg is available in 12 languages: Vietnamese, English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Arabic, Russian, Japanese, and Korean. Use the language switcher at the top of the page to change languages.
faq.q6: Do I need an account to use Dealeg?
faq.a6: No account is needed to browse and use coupon codes. However, creating a free account lets you comment, vote on whether codes work, and save your favorite deals. You can sign in with Google, Facebook, GitHub, or email.
faq.a7: When you click a link and make a purchase, we may earn a commission from the merchant. This never costs you more — the price is the same. These commissions keep Dealeg free to use. We recommend products honestly regardless of commission. See our Affiliate Disclosure for details.
faq.q8: Can I submit a coupon or report an expired one?
faq.a8: Yes! Use the "Submit" page to share a coupon you found, or vote on existing coupons to tell the community whether they still work. This helps keep our information accurate for everyone.

qr.intro: A WiFi QR code stores your network name, password and security type in the standard WIFI: format that phone cameras read natively, so guests connect by pointing a camera instead of typing — or ever seeing — the password. The contact tab does the same for a vCard. Everything is generated in your browser, so the password never leaves your device.
qr.step1: Choose the WiFi tab for a network code, or the contact tab for a vCard.
qr.step2: For WiFi, type the network name exactly as it appears: SSIDs are case-sensitive and spaces count. Then add the password and pick the security type — WPA/WPA2 for essentially every modern router, WEP only for very old equipment, or none for an open network.
qr.step3: Tick “hidden network” only if your router does not broadcast its name; ticking it for a normal network stops the scan from working.
qr.step4: The code updates as you type. Scan it with your own phone once to confirm it connects before you print or share it.
qr.q1: Is my WiFi password sent to a server?
qr.a1: No. The code is built entirely in your browser and nothing is uploaded. You can prove it to yourself: load the page, disconnect from the internet, and the generator still works.
qr.q2: Which phones can scan a WiFi QR without installing an app?
qr.a2: The built-in camera on iPhone (iOS 11 and later) and on most Android 10 and newer devices recognises WIFI: codes and offers to join the network. Older Android phones may still need a separate QR scanner.
qr.q3: The code scans but will not connect — why?
qr.a3: Almost always one of three things: the network name has different capitalisation or a stray space, the security type is wrong (WPA2 chosen for a WEP network or the reverse), or the network is hidden and the box was left unticked.
qr.tip: For a café, office or guest network, print the code and leave it on the table. Visitors get online without anyone reading a password out loud, and when you change the password you simply regenerate the code.

password.intro: This generator draws from the browser's cryptographic random source (crypto.getRandomValues) rather than the ordinary Math.random that many web generators use and that can be predicted from earlier output. Passwords are assembled on your device and are never transmitted.
password.step1: Set the length. Sixteen characters is a sensible floor, and longer is genuinely stronger.
password.step2: Choose which character sets to draw from: uppercase, lowercase, digits and symbols.
password.step3: Press Generate, then Copy, and paste the result straight into your password manager instead of retyping it.
password.q1: Is it safe to generate a password on a website?
password.a1: The work here happens in your browser, so nothing is sent anywhere. Even so, the safest habit is to let your password manager generate and store passwords for you; use a page like this when you do not have one to hand.
password.q2: How long should a password actually be?
password.a2: Sixteen random characters drawn from three or more character sets is far beyond the reach of brute force today. Length does more work than complexity: a long password of plain letters beats a short one crammed with symbols.
password.q3: A site rejected my password — what should I do?
password.a3: Some older systems refuse particular symbols or cap the length. Generate a fresh one with symbols switched off or a shorter length rather than editing the password by hand, because manual edits remove the randomness that makes it strong.
password.tip: Never reuse a password across sites, and change one the moment a service reports a breach. Reuse is what turns a single company's leak into a problem on every account you own.

discount.intro: Two calculations on one page: work out what you actually pay once a percentage comes off, or work backwards from an original and a sale price to find the real discount. The second is the useful one for checking whether an advertised offer is as generous as the sign claims.
discount.step1: In the first box, enter the original price and the discount percentage to get the final price and the amount saved.
discount.step2: In the second box, enter the original price and the price you are actually being offered to get the true percentage off.
discount.step3: Amounts are formatted for your language automatically, so large numbers stay readable at a glance.
discount.q1: Two discounts are advertised together — do they add up?
discount.a1: No, they multiply. Twenty percent off followed by a further ten percent is 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, which is 28 percent off rather than 30. To do it here, take the final price from the first calculation and enter it as the original price for the second.
discount.q2: How can I tell whether a discount is genuine?
discount.a2: Use the second box with the price you can actually see today. If the percentage it returns is well below the advertised one, the “original” price is doing the marketing. Checking the same item at another retailer is the quickest sanity check.
discount.q3: Does the result include tax or VAT?
discount.a3: It works on whatever number you type. If the price you enter already includes VAT then the final price does too; if it excludes VAT, so does the result.
discount.tip: For subscriptions, apply the discount across the whole period you actually intend to stay, not the headline monthly price. “Half price for the first year” on a service you keep for two years is about twenty-five percent off overall.

base64.intro: Encodes text to Base64 and decodes it back, handling Unicode correctly — including Vietnamese accents, which many simpler implementations mangle into question marks.
base64.step1: Paste your text, or the Base64 string you want to read.
base64.q1: Is Base64 a form of encryption?
base64.a1: No, and the distinction matters. It is an encoding that anyone can reverse instantly, so it must never be used to hide a password, a token or personal data.
base64.a2: Carrying binary or non-ASCII content through channels that only accept plain text: email attachments, data URLs, and values embedded in configuration files or tokens.
base64.q3: Why do other tools break Vietnamese text?
base64.a3: They call the browser's btoa directly, which only accepts single-byte characters. The text has to be encoded as UTF-8 first, which is the step this tool performs for you.
base64.tip: Base64 makes data roughly a third larger. That is harmless for short strings, but embedding a sizeable image as a data URL is usually slower than simply linking to the file.

currency.intro: Converts between twenty widely used currencies with reference rates refreshed once a day. These are mid-market rates — the number quoted in the news — not the rate a bank or card will actually give you, which is exactly what makes them useful as a baseline.
currency.step1: Choose the currency you are converting from and to.
currency.step2: Type the amount; the result updates as you type.
currency.step3: Use swap to reverse the direction without retyping.
currency.q1: Why is my bank's rate worse?
currency.a1: Banks, exchange counters and card networks add a spread, typically half a percent to three percent, and sometimes a fixed fee on top. Comparing their quote against the mid-market rate here tells you the real cost of the transaction.
currency.a2: They refresh daily from open.er-api.com. That is fine for budgeting, planning a trip or sanity-checking a quote, but it is not a trading feed.
currency.q3: Is cash or card better abroad?
currency.a3: Card networks convert close to the mid-market rate plus a small fee, which usually beats cash bought at an airport counter. Withdrawing local currency from an ATM often beats both.
currency.tip: When a foreign card machine offers to charge you in your home currency, decline it. That convenience is dynamic currency conversion, and the markup buried in it is usually several percent.

datecalc.intro: Two related calculations: exact age in years, months and days from a date of birth, and the distance between any two dates in days and weeks. Leap years are handled properly, including a 29 February birthday.
datecalc.step1: Choose the age tab or the date difference tab.
datecalc.step2: Enter the date of birth, or the two dates you want to measure between.
datecalc.step3: Read the breakdown in years, months and days, or in total days and weeks.
datecalc.q1: Why does age need months and days as well as years?
datecalc.a1: Visa rules, insurance bands and school entry cut-offs frequently depend on exact age on a particular day, where being a few weeks either side of a birthday changes the answer.
datecalc.a2: The difference counts the days between the two dates. If you need to count both endpoints, such as the length of a stay including the day of arrival, add one to the result.
datecalc.a3: They are counted correctly, so periods spanning 29 February come out right and a person born on that date ages normally.
datecalc.tip: Deadlines quoted in working days need one more step: this gives total days, and you subtract weekends and public holidays yourself, since those differ by country and by year.

grossnet.intro: Converts salary in both directions under Vietnam's personal income tax rules for tax year 2026: the five-bracket table, the 15.5 million personal and 6.2 million per-dependent deductions, and the 46.8 million cap on the social and health insurance base.
grossnet.step1: Choose whether you are starting from gross or from net.
grossnet.step2: Enter the salary figure and the number of dependents you register.
grossnet.step3: Pick your region, which sets the ceiling used for unemployment insurance.
grossnet.step4: Read the breakdown: insurance contributions, deductions, taxable income and the tax itself.
grossnet.q1: Why does this differ from my payslip?
grossnet.a1: The calculator assumes your whole salary is the insurance base, while many contracts declare a lower insured amount. Allowances for lunch, phone or travel are also partly exempt, so real payslips usually land slightly higher.
grossnet.q2: What does the region setting change?
grossnet.a2: Regional minimum wage sets the ceiling for unemployment insurance, so moving between regions changes that contribution and therefore the net figure a little.
grossnet.q3: Does it cover bonuses or the thirteenth month?
grossnet.a3: No. Those are taxed in the month they are paid and can push that month into a higher bracket. For an estimate, add the bonus to that single month's gross and run it again.
grossnet.tip: When negotiating, agree the NET figure if you want certainty about what reaches your account — gross moves with dependants and insurance rules, net is what you actually live on.

hash.intro: Produces SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 hashes of whatever you type, using the browser's built-in Web Crypto implementation. The text never leaves your device.
hash.step1: Type or paste the text you want to hash.
hash.step2: Read the hashes, which update as you type.
hash.q1: What is a hash actually for?
hash.a1: Checking that something has not changed. Compare a published checksum against the one you compute yourself, and any difference at all means the content is not what was published.
hash.q2: Can the original text be recovered?
hash.a2: Not by reversing it — hashing is one-way by design. But short or common inputs can be found in precomputed lookup tables, so a hash on its own is not a way to keep a secret.
hash.a3: Only for compatibility with older systems that require it. Practical collision attacks against SHA-1 have existed for years, so anything new should use SHA-256 or stronger.
hash.tip: Hashing a password with plain SHA is not secure storage. Password systems need a deliberately slow algorithm with a per-user salt — bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 — precisely because SHA is fast.

idphoto.intro: Crops a photograph to the Vietnamese ID sizes of 3×4 or 4×6 centimetres at 300 DPI, the resolution print shops expect, on a white or blue background. The image is processed on your device and is never uploaded, which matters for a document photo.
idphoto.step1: Choose a photo from your device and pick the size you need.
idphoto.step2: Drag to position the face and use the zoom slider until the head fills the frame properly.
idphoto.step3: Select a white or blue background to match what the document requires.
idphoto.step4: Download the result and take the file to a print shop, or print at 300 DPI.
idphoto.q1: How should the face be framed?
idphoto.a1: Face the camera straight on with a neutral expression, both eyebrows and ears visible, and the head occupying roughly three quarters of the frame height. Always check the exact rule for the document you are applying for.
idphoto.a2: Vietnamese identity documents commonly use blue or white, while most visa applications insist on plain white. The issuing authority's own guidance is the only thing that settles it.
idphoto.q3: Can I just print it at home?
idphoto.a3: The file is 300 DPI, which is enough for a photo lab. Home printers on ordinary paper rarely meet the paper and finish requirements for official submissions.
idphoto.tip: Photograph yourself against a plain wall in soft daylight, without flash and standing far enough from the wall to avoid a hard shadow. Good capture saves far more trouble than any amount of editing afterwards.

imagecompress.intro: Re-encodes images at a quality you choose and converts between JPG, WebP and PNG, entirely inside your browser with nothing uploaded. Original and compressed sizes are shown side by side so you can judge the trade-off yourself.
imagecompress.step1: Select an image from your device.
imagecompress.step2: Choose the output format you want.
imagecompress.step3: Move the quality slider and watch the compressed size respond.
imagecompress.step4: Download once the size and the appearance both look acceptable.
imagecompress.a1: WebP is typically twenty-five to thirty-five percent smaller than JPG at comparable quality and is supported by every current browser. Keep PNG only for screenshots, logos, line art and anything that needs transparency.
imagecompress.a2: Between 75 and 85 suits photographs. Below about 60, blocking and halos around sharp edges become visible, and text inside an image degrades first.
imagecompress.a3: Yes — this is lossy re-encoding, so keep your original. Repeatedly compressing an already compressed file degrades it each time, even at a high quality setting.
imagecompress.tip: Resize before you compress. An image displayed 800 pixels wide gains far more from being saved at 800 pixels than from any amount of slider adjustment at full resolution.

interest.intro: Two calculations in one place: what a loan costs each month under either declining balance or equal instalments, and what savings grow to with simple or compound interest. Both show the totals, which is where the real differences appear.
interest.step1: Choose the loan or the savings tab.
interest.step2: Enter the amount, the annual rate and the term in months.
interest.step3: For a loan, pick declining balance or equal payments.
interest.step4: Compare the first and last payment, the total interest and the total paid.
interest.q1: Declining balance or equal payments — which costs less?
interest.a1: Declining balance almost always costs less overall, because interest is charged only on what you still owe, but the early payments are the highest. Equal instalments cost more in total and are easier to budget around.
interest.q2: Why does my bank quote a higher figure?
interest.a2: This excludes arrangement fees, compulsory insurance and early repayment penalties. Many advertised rates are also promotional for the first several months and then float to a considerably higher one.
interest.a3: Simple interest pays only on the original sum. Compound adds each period's interest back so it earns in turn, and over long terms the gap between the two becomes very large.
interest.tip: Judge a loan by the total you will hand over, not the monthly payment. Stretching the term always lowers the monthly figure while quietly increasing the total cost.

json.intro: Formats JSON with indentation so it can be read, minifies it back down to the smallest valid form, and tells you where the problem is when it will not parse. Everything runs in your browser.
json.step1: Paste your JSON into the input area.
json.step2: Press format to indent it, or minify to strip every unnecessary character.
json.step3: If it reports an error, fix the position it points to and try again.
json.a1: Almost always one of four things: a trailing comma after the last item, single quotes instead of double, keys left unquoted, or a comment. JSON permits none of them, however reasonable they look.
json.a2: No, it only removes whitespace. A parser reads the minified and the formatted version identically; the difference is purely how many bytes travel over the network.
json.q3: Is my data sent to a server?
json.a3: No, it is parsed in your browser, so it is safe to paste payloads containing API keys or personal data — something worth checking before using any online formatter.
json.tip: When a large document fails, paste it in halves to find the broken part. Reported error positions in big files are frequently a long way from the mistake that actually caused them.

lunar.intro: Converts dates between the solar calendar and the Vietnamese lunar calendar in both directions, leap months included. It is the calculation behind death anniversaries, Tết, and the traditional dates that shift against the solar calendar every year.
lunar.step1: Choose whether you are converting solar to lunar or the reverse.
lunar.step2: Enter the day, month and year.
lunar.step3: Tick the leap flag if the lunar month you are entering is a leap month.
lunar.q1: Is the Vietnamese lunar calendar the same as the Chinese one?
lunar.a1: They are very close but not identical. Vietnam computes its calendar on UTC+7 and China on UTC+8, so a given date can differ by a day, and occasionally Tết and Chinese New Year fall on different days.
lunar.a2: A lunar year runs about eleven days shorter than a solar year, so roughly every three years an extra month is inserted to keep the seasons aligned. It repeats the previous month's number and is marked as leap.
lunar.q3: Why does a lunar birthday move every year?
lunar.a3: Because a fixed lunar date maps onto a different solar date each year. That is exactly why anniversaries and giỗ appear to wander across the calendar.
lunar.tip: For a recurring anniversary, convert it once each year and put that solar date in your phone. A yearly repeating reminder set on the solar date will drift away from the lunar one almost immediately.

num2words.intro: Spells an amount out in words in both Vietnamese and English — the wording invoices, contracts and cheques require, so a figure cannot be altered afterwards by adding a digit.
num2words.step1: Type the number you need spelled out.
num2words.step2: Read the Vietnamese and English wording produced.
num2words.step3: Copy the version you need into your document.
num2words.q1: Why do invoices need the amount in words?
num2words.a1: It is a fraud control. Digits can be edited convincingly, a written phrase cannot, and Vietnamese accounting practice expects both to appear and to agree with each other.
num2words.q2: How are awkward numbers read in Vietnamese?
num2words.a2: Empty groups take lẻ or linh, and depending on position một becomes mốt, bốn becomes tư and năm becomes lăm. Those rules are applied for you, which is where most hand-written attempts go wrong.
num2words.a3: It is built for whole currency amounts, which is what contracts use. Round to the nearest unit before entering the figure.
num2words.tip: Paste the wording exactly as produced and add the currency word after it. Retyping or tidying the phrase by hand is precisely how the words end up disagreeing with the digits.

pdf.intro: Combines several PDFs into one file, or pulls a range of pages out of a document, on your own device. The files are never uploaded, which is the difference that matters when the document is a contract, a payslip or an identity paper.
pdf.step1: Choose whether you are merging or splitting.
pdf.step2: To merge, add the files in the order you want them to appear.
pdf.step3: To split, enter the pages you need using a range such as 1-3,5.
pdf.step4: Download the result and check it before sending it on.
pdf.q1: Is this safe for confidential documents?
pdf.a1: The processing happens in your browser, so the file never leaves your computer. Most free online PDF services upload your document to a server instead, which is a meaningful difference for anything sensitive.
pdf.q2: Can it open a password-protected PDF?
pdf.a2: No. Remove the password in whatever application created or opened the file first, otherwise processing will simply fail.
pdf.q3: Why did my file fail to process?
pdf.a3: Usually the PDF is password-protected or damaged, or the page range falls outside the document — asking for page twelve of a ten-page file, for instance.
pdf.tip: Always open the merged file and check the page order before sending it. Merging follows the order the files were added, which is not always the order you thought you picked them in.

textcounter.intro: Counts words, characters with and without spaces, and lines as you type, and converts text between uppercase, lowercase, title case and sentence case. Useful whenever something has a hard limit attached to it.
textcounter.step1: Paste or type your text into the box.
textcounter.step2: Read the counters, which update immediately.
textcounter.step3: Press a case button to transform the text, then copy the result.
textcounter.q1: Which count do platforms actually use?
textcounter.a1: Nearly every published limit — social posts, SMS, meta descriptions, form fields — counts characters including spaces. Word counts matter mainly for essays, briefs and editorial guidelines.
textcounter.a2: Any run of characters between spaces, so e-mail counts as one word while e mail counts as two. Hyphenation therefore changes the total.
textcounter.q3: Why do Vietnamese text messages run out so fast?
textcounter.a3: A plain message fits 160 characters per segment, but a single accented character switches the whole message to Unicode encoding, which cuts each segment to 70.
textcounter.tip: For search results, aim at roughly 150 to 160 characters for a meta description and about 60 for a title. Past those points Google simply cuts the text off mid-sentence.

unitprice.intro: Works out the price per unit for two options so you can see which is genuinely cheaper — the comparison shops make difficult by selling similar products in deliberately different pack sizes.
unitprice.step1: Enter the price and the quantity or weight for product A.
unitprice.step2: Do the same for product B, using the same unit for both.
unitprice.step3: Read the price per unit; the cheaper option is marked for you.
unitprice.q1: Is the larger pack always better value?
unitprice.a1: Usually, but far from always. Promotions on small packs and premium pricing on so-called value packs both reverse the maths regularly, which is the whole reason to check.
unitprice.q2: What if the units are different?
unitprice.a2: Convert them to the same unit before entering, so 1.5 kg becomes 1500 g. Comparing grams against kilograms produces a number that looks authoritative and means nothing.
unitprice.q3: What about what I will not use?
unitprice.a3: Cheaper per unit is only cheaper if it gets used. For anything perishable, judge the size against what you will realistically get through before it spoils.
unitprice.tip: Photograph the shelf labels and compare afterwards. Shelf tags do show unit prices, but different brands are often measured per 100 g, per kilogram or per item, which makes them useless side by side.

utm.intro: Builds a link carrying UTM parameters so your analytics can attribute a visit to a specific campaign, channel and piece of creative, instead of filing it under direct traffic where it tells you nothing.
utm.step1: Paste the destination URL on your own site.
utm.step2: Fill in the source, meaning where the link is published, and the medium, meaning what kind of channel that is.
utm.step3: Give the campaign a name you will still recognise in six months.
utm.step4: Add term or content only when you are splitting variants, then copy the finished link.
utm.q1: What is the difference between source and medium?
utm.a1: Source is the specific place — facebook, newsletter, a partner site. Medium is the category that place belongs to — social, email, cpc, referral. Agreeing a convention and sticking to it matters more than which words you pick.
utm.a2: Very much. Analytics treats Facebook and facebook as two separate sources, which quietly splits one campaign across two rows in every report. Use lowercase everywhere.
utm.q3: Should I tag links inside my own website?
utm.a3: No. Tagging internal links starts a new session and reassigns the credit, which destroys the attribution you were trying to measure. UTMs belong only on links pointing in from outside.
utm.tip: Keep a single spreadsheet listing the exact source, medium and campaign values you have used. After a few months that document is worth more than any individual link, because it is what makes old reports comparable.

vietqr.intro: A VietQR code carries your bank, account number and optionally a fixed amount and transfer note, so the payer scans instead of retyping an account number — which is where most failed or misdirected transfers begin. It follows the Napas standard every Vietnamese banking app reads.
vietqr.step1: Pick your bank and type the account number exactly, with no spaces.
vietqr.step2: Add the account holder name so the payer can confirm they have the right person before sending.
vietqr.step3: Optionally lock an amount and a transfer note; leave the amount blank if the payer should decide it.
vietqr.step4: Download the code and put it on an invoice, a storefront sign or a message.
vietqr.q1: Do I have to fill in the amount?
vietqr.a1: No. Leave it blank and the payer enters it themselves, which suits donations or variable bills. Fill it in for a fixed-price item so the sum cannot be mistyped.
vietqr.q2: Which apps can scan this code?
vietqr.a2: Any Vietnamese banking app that supports VietQR — that covers all the major banks — plus e-wallets that read the Napas format.
vietqr.q3: Is it safe to share my account number?
vietqr.a3: An account number and holder name are what you would print on an invoice anyway; they let people send money to you, not take it. What must never be shared is an OTP or your banking login.
vietqr.tip: For a shop, print one code with no amount but with your shop name pre-filled as the transfer note. It then appears on every incoming line in your statement, which makes reconciling the day's takings far quicker.

vnfont.intro: Vietnamese documents typed years ago in TCVN3 (ABC) fonts turn into gibberish on modern computers, because the file stores one set of byte values while the system renders them with a Unicode font. This converts that text to proper Unicode, and can also strip accents when you need plain ASCII.
vnfont.step1: Paste the broken text into the input box.
vnfont.step2: Read the converted Unicode result, which you can copy straight into any modern editor.
vnfont.step3: Switch on remove accents if you need an unaccented version as well.
vnfont.q1: Why does old text look like a jumble of symbols?
vnfont.a1: The bytes are TCVN3 codes but your system draws them with a Unicode font, so every byte lands on the wrong glyph. Nothing is corrupted — the text just needs remapping, which is what this does.
vnfont.q2: Does it handle VNI or VISCII too?
vnfont.a2: Not yet; it covers TCVN3, which is by far the most common legacy encoding in Vietnamese documents. VNI support is planned. If particular characters come out wrong, report them through the contact page.
vnfont.q3: Why would I want to remove accents?
vnfont.a3: Unaccented text is safer for file names, URL slugs, and older systems that reject anything outside ASCII — bank transfer notes and some government forms among them.
vnfont.tip: Convert the whole document before you start editing it. Once corrected and uncorrected passages are mixed together in one file, separating them again is painful.
